questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate action.

cells: Dark pigment in palm creases and gums

rationale.correct: Shock, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and hyponatremia after missed steroid doses is adrenal crisis.

perOption.r2: Hyperkalemia from aldosterone deficiency; dysrhythmia risk.
perOption.r6: A chronic sign of primary adrenal insufficiency, not acute.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the missing hormone mainly responsible.

rows.text: Hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia
Hyponatremia and volume loss
Hypotension that does not respond to fluids alone
Darkened skin

rationale.correct: Primary adrenal insufficiency lacks both cortisol and aldosterone, and high ACTH darkens the skin.

perOption.r2:c1: Aldosterone makes the kidney excrete potassium.
perOption.r2:c2: Aldosterone makes the kidney excrete potassium.
perOption.r2:c3: Aldosterone makes the kidney excrete potassium.
perOption.r4:c1: Cortisol is needed for vessels to respond to catecholamines.
perOption.r4:c2: Cortisol is needed for vessels to respond to catecholamines.
perOption.r4:c3: Cortisol is needed for vessels to respond to catecholamines.
perOption.r5:c1: ACTH stimulates melanocytes in primary adrenal failure.
perOption.r5:c2: ACTH stimulates melanocytes in primary adrenal failure.
perOption.r5:c3: ACTH stimulates melanocytes in primary adrenal failure.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: The client is in {{b1}}, triggered by {{b2}}, and the most immediate threats are {{b3}}.

rationale.correct: Adrenal crisis from missed doses during illness; shock and hyperkalemia are the immediate threats.

perOption.b1:b: Infection may contribute, but the electrolytes point to adrenal crisis.
perOption.b2:a: Illness raises cortisol needs while doses were lost.
perOption.b3:c: A symptom, not the main threat.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: For each order, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

rows.text: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV now
0.9% sodium chloride 1 L rapidly
Dextrose for the glucose of 54 mg/dL
Wait for a cortisol level before giving steroids
Potassium chloride with the fluids
Cardiac monitoring

rationale.correct: Give IV hydrocortisone at once, saline and dextrose, and monitor the heart; do not delay for tests.

perOption.r1:c1: Replaces cortisol; at this dose it also has mineralocorticoid effect.
perOption.r1:c2: Replaces cortisol; at this dose it also has mineralocorticoid effect.
perOption.r4:c1: Draw blood if possible, but never delay treatment.
perOption.r4:c2: Draw blood if possible, but never delay treatment.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Generate the treatment for adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: Review the findings 4 hours after treatment. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continue hydrocortisone every 6 hours as prescribed
Report the sodium rise of 12 mEq/L in 4 hours
Stop the steroid now that blood pressure is normal
Give fludrocortisone instead of hydrocortisone tonight

rationale.correct: Continue stress-dose steroids, keep checking electrolytes, and report a sodium rise that is too fast.

perOption.d: Stopping would bring the crisis back.
perOption.e: High-dose hydrocortisone already covers mineralocorticoid needs.

questions.educationalObjective: Take action during recovery from adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: Before discharge, the client describes sick-day rules. For each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "With a fever, I'll double my hydrocortisone doses."
"If I'm vomiting and can't keep tablets down, I'll inject the emergency hydrocortisone and go to the ED."
"I'll wear a medical alert bracelet."
"I'll double the fludrocortisone too when I'm sick."
"If I feel well, I can skip the afternoon dose."
"I'll tell any surgeon or dentist that I take steroids."

rationale.correct: Sick-day rules: increase hydrocortisone, inject when vomiting, wear ID, never skip doses.

perOption.r2:c1: The emergency kit prevents a crisis.
perOption.r2:c2: The emergency kit prevents a crisis.
perOption.r4:c1: Stress dosing applies to hydrocortisone, not fludrocortisone.
perOption.r4:c2: Stress dosing applies to hydrocortisone, not fludrocortisone.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are effects of long-term glucocorticoid therapy.

segments.text: a round face and a fat pad between the shoulders
thin, bruised skin with purple stretch marks

rationale.correct: Fat redistribution, skin fragility, proximal myopathy and hyperglycemia are signs of Cushing syndrome.

perOption.s8: From pneumonia, not a steroid effect, though steroids raise infection risk.
perOption.s12: A consequence of myopathy and a safety concern, rather than a direct sign.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether it is accurate or inaccurate.

rows.text: The normal temperature rules out a serious infection
The low potassium is a steroid effect
The client's own adrenal glands are probably suppressed
Prednisone can be stopped now because of the infection
The WBC of 16,800 may partly reflect the steroid

rationale.correct: Steroids mask fever, waste potassium, suppress the adrenals and raise the WBC.

perOption.r1:c1: Steroids blunt fever; the WBC and x-ray show pneumonia.
perOption.r1:c2: Steroids blunt fever; the WBC and x-ray show pneumonia.
perOption.r3:c1: Months of prednisone suppress ACTH and cortisol production.
perOption.r3:c2: Months of prednisone suppress ACTH and cortisol production.
perOption.r5:c1: Steroids raise neutrophil counts, so infection is judged on the whole picture.
perOption.r5:c2: Steroids raise neutrophil counts, so infection is judged on the whole picture.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze the effects of chronic steroid therapy.

questions.stem: For each risk, indicate its priority during this admission.

rows.text: Adrenal crisis if a dose is missed while ill
Worsening pneumonia hidden by the steroid
Falls and fracture
Hyperglycemia
Cosmetic changes

rationale.correct: Adrenal suppression, masked infection, falls and hyperglycemia are the main risks.

perOption.r1:c1: Illness raises the need for steroid.
perOption.r1:c2: Illness raises the need for steroid.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize risks of chronic steroid therapy.

questions.stem: Which parts of the plan should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continue prednisone; the provider may increase it during the illness
A bone density scan and calcium with vitamin D
Stop prednisone at once to help fight the infection
Rely on the temperature to judge whether the antibiotic is working

rationale.correct: Continue or stress-dose the steroid and treat its effects: glucose, potassium and bone.

perOption.b: Steroid hyperglycemia peaks in the afternoon.

questions.educationalObjective: Generate a plan for a client on long-term steroids.

exhibits.title: Orders
exhibits.body: Ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Prednisone 30 mg daily. Insulin correction scale. Potassium chloride 40 mEq PO.

questions.stem: For each safety risk, select the actions the nurse should take.

options.text: A raised chair or toilet seat and grab bars
Keep the client on bed rest to avoid falls
Use a lift sheet when repositioning
Pad the bed rails and avoid tape on the skin
Strict hand hygiene by staff and visitors
Avoid rooming the client with someone who has an infection
Give live vaccines while in hospital

rationale.correct: Prevent falls, protect fragile skin and reduce infection exposure.

perOption.i: Live vaccines are avoided on high-dose steroids.

exhibits.body: Able to walk with a walker and one assist. Skin tear on the forearm from a blood pressure cuff.

questions.stem: The rheumatologist plans to taper the prednisone. For each statement by the client, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "I'll lower the dose slowly on the schedule, not stop it suddenly."
"If I feel weak, dizzy or sick while tapering, I'll call."
"I'll take prednisone in the morning with food."
"Once I'm off it, my face will go back to normal within a week."
"I'll skip my dose if my blood sugar is high."
"I'll tell any doctor I've taken steroids in the past year."

rationale.correct: Teaching covers slow tapering, warning signs, morning dosing with food and never skipping.

perOption.r3:c1: Matches the body's rhythm and protects the stomach.
perOption.r3:c2: Matches the body's rhythm and protects the stomach.
perOption.r5:c1: Never skip; call about high glucose.
perOption.r5:c2: Never skip; call about high glucose.
perOption.r6:c1: Stress dosing may still be needed.
perOption.r6:c2: Stress dosing may still be needed.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of severe hyponatremia.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it supports SIADH.

rows.text: Low serum osmolality
Concentrated urine (osmolality 560)
High urine sodium (62)
Normal thyroid and adrenal function
Edema and crackles

rationale.correct: SIADH: dilute blood, inappropriately concentrated urine, high urine sodium, no edema, normal thyroid and adrenals.

perOption.r2:c1: ADH keeps the kidneys holding water.
perOption.r2:c2: ADH keeps the kidneys holding water.
perOption.r5:c1: SIADH causes water gain without edema; edema suggests heart failure or cirrhosis.
perOption.r5:c2: SIADH causes water gain without edema; edema suggests heart failure or cirrhosis.

options.text: a small rise in sodium to stop seizures

rationale.correct: Tumor ADH causes SIADH; raise sodium a little to stop seizures, then correct slowly.

perOption.b2:a: A few mEq/L reduces cerebral edema.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize treatment in symptomatic SIADH.

questions.stem: For each order, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

rows.text: 3% sodium chloride 100 mL IV bolus, repeated if seizures continue
Sodium checks every 2 hours
Seizure precautions
Fluid restriction once stable
0.9% sodium chloride 2 L rapidly
Free water flushes with tube feeds

rationale.correct: Hypertonic saline in small boluses with close sodium checks; isotonic saline and free water can worsen SIADH.

perOption.r5:c1: In SIADH, the sodium is excreted and the water kept, which can lower sodium further.
perOption.r5:c2: In SIADH, the sodium is excreted and the water kept, which can lower sodium further.

exhibits.title: Orders, 1410
exhibits.body: 3% sodium chloride 100 mL over 10 minutes; may repeat twice. Sodium every 2 hours. Seizure precautions. Fluid restriction 1 L/day when stable.

questions.stem: Review the sodium trend. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Report the sodium rise to the provider now
Anticipate D5W or desmopressin to slow or reverse the rise
Continue the current plan because the client is awake
Give a second 3% bolus to reach normal sodium

rationale.correct: Overcorrection of chronic hyponatremia must be stopped and sometimes reversed to prevent osmotic demyelination.

perOption.a: A rise of 12 mEq/L in 10 hours is above the safe limit.
perOption.c: Large urine output can raise sodium quickly.
perOption.d: Used to re-lower sodium when overcorrection occurs.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it fits diabetes insipidus or SIADH.

rows.text: Large volumes of dilute urine
Serum sodium 151 mEq/L
Concentrated urine with low serum sodium
Weight gain without edema
Intense thirst

rationale.correct: DI loses water (high sodium, dilute urine); SIADH keeps water (low sodium, concentrated urine).

questions.stem: Which orders should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hourly urine output and specific gravity
Let the client drink to thirst
Fluid restriction to 1 L a day
Encourage the client to blow the nose to clear the drip

rationale.correct: Desmopressin with close output and sodium monitoring; let the client drink, and protect the surgical site.

perOption.c: Guards against both hypernatremia and overcorrection.
perOption.f: Raises pressure and worsens a CSF leak.

questions.educationalObjective: Generate the plan for postoperative DI.

exhibits.title: Orders, 0700
exhibits.body: Desmopressin 1 mcg IV. Test nasal drainage for glucose. Head of bed 30 degrees.

questions.stem: Which instructions and actions should the nurse give the client now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Do not blow your nose, cough hard or bend over
Do not use a straw or brush your teeth until cleared
Report a headache or stiff neck
Lie flat to stop the drip
Use a nasal decongestant spray if the nose feels blocked

rationale.correct: Protect the transsphenoidal site and watch for meningitis while a CSF leak is assessed.

perOption.a: Prevents pressure on the surgical site.
perOption.c: Protects the incision under the upper lip.
perOption.d: Possible meningitis with a CSF leak.
perOption.e: The head of the bed is raised.

questions.stem: Review the findings on day 3. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.

rows.text: Urine output 80 to 120 mL/hour; specific gravity 1.015
Nasal drip has stopped
Sodium 128 mEq/L after two more desmopressin doses
Temperature 38.5 C (101.3 F), headache and neck stiffness
Endocrinology has reviewed the cortisol and thyroid plan

rationale.correct: DI and the leak have improved, but low sodium from desmopressin and signs of meningitis need urgent action.

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0400
exhibits.body: A 38-year-old client with Addison disease takes hydrocortisone 15 mg in the morning and 5 mg in the afternoon, and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. For 2 days the client has had vomiting and diarrhea and could not keep tablets down. The client did not have an injectable hydrocortisone kit. Now the client is weak, confused and has severe abdominal pain. Skin is darkly pigmented in the palm creases and gums.

exhibits.title: Medical unit, admission
exhibits.body: A 62-year-old client has taken prednisone 30 mg daily for 8 months for polymyalgia. The client is admitted with a productive cough but no fever. Findings: round face, fat pad between the shoulders, thin skin with bruises, purple stretch marks on the abdomen, and weak thigh muscles (cannot rise from a chair without using the arms). The client fell at home last week.

exhibits.title: Oncology unit, 1400
exhibits.body: A 66-year-old client with small cell lung cancer has had nausea and headache for 3 days and is now confused. Weight is up 2 kg with no edema. At 1400 the client has a generalized seizure lasting 90 seconds. Weight 70 kg.

exhibits.title: Neurosurgical unit, postoperative day 1
exhibits.body: A 47-year-old client had transsphenoidal removal of a pituitary adenoma yesterday. Nasal packing is in place. Since midnight the client has passed large amounts of pale urine and is very thirsty. The client reports clear, watery drip from the nose when leaning forward.

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
